rewritten_text:
Great God! Had I guessed my enemy's dreadful plan for even a moment, I would have left my country forever and wandered the earth without a friend rather than agree to this unhappy marriage. But the monster seemed to have used magic to hide his true purpose from me. Thinking I had arranged only my own death, I brought nearer the death of someone far dearer.

As our wedding approached, my heart grew heavy, whether through cowardice or some warning instinct. I hid my feelings behind a cheerful manner. This made my father smile with happiness, but barely deceived Elizabeth, who watched me more closely and understood me better. She looked forward to our marriage with quiet contentment, though past sorrows had left her a little afraid. Happiness now seemed real and certain, yet she feared it might vanish like a dream, leaving only deep and lasting regret.

We prepared for the wedding and received visits from people bringing congratulations. Everything appeared happy. I kept my gnawing anxiety hidden as well as I could and seemed to join eagerly in my father's plans, though they might merely provide the setting for my tragedy. Through his efforts, the Austrian government had returned part of Elizabeth's inheritance. She owned a small property beside Lake Como. We agreed to go to Villa Lavenza immediately after the ceremony and spend our first happy days together beside the beautiful lake near the villa.

Meanwhile, I did everything possible to protect myself in case the monster attacked openly. I always carried pistols and a dagger and watched constantly for tricks. These precautions made me calmer. Indeed, as the wedding came closer, the threat began to seem like an illusion unworthy of disturbing my peace. The happiness I expected from marriage felt increasingly certain. The date approached, and I heard everyone speak of the wedding as something no accident could possibly prevent.

Elizabeth seemed happy, and my calm behaviour did much to quiet her worries. Yet on the day that would fulfil both my wishes and my destiny, she was sad and filled with a sense that something terrible was coming. Perhaps she was also thinking of the dreadful secret I had promised to tell her the next day.

The following day the ghost was exhausted and weak. The terrible strain of the past four weeks was finally catching up with him. His nerves were in ruins, and every small sound made him start. He stayed in his room for five days before deciding to abandon the bloodstain on the library floor. If the Otises did not want it, they clearly did not deserve it. Obviously they existed on a crude, material level and were incapable of appreciating the symbolic significance of sensory phenomena. Ghostly manifestations and the formation of astral bodies were another matter entirely, of course, and not truly within his control. He was solemnly obliged to appear in the corridor each week and to gibber from the great oriel window on the first and third Wednesdays of every month. He could find no honourable way around these duties. His life had certainly been wicked, yet in all supernatural matters he was exceptionally conscientious. Accordingly, on the next three Saturdays he made his usual passage along the corridor between midnight and three, doing everything possible to avoid being seen or heard. He took off his boots, walked softly over the worm-eaten boards, wrapped himself in a large black velvet cloak, and carefully applied Rising Sun Lubricator to his chains. I must acknowledge that accepting this last form of protection cost him considerable effort. Nevertheless, one night while the family was dining, he crept into Mr. Otis's bedroom and stole the bottle. He initially felt somewhat humiliated, but afterward had the sense to admit that the invention had considerable merits and served his purpose to a degree. Despite all these precautions, he was still harassed. Someone continually stretched strings across the corridor, tripping him in the dark. Once, dressed as 'Black Isaac, or the Huntsman of Hogley Woods,' he fell heavily after stepping onto a butter slide the twins had laid between the Tapestry Chamber door and the head of the oak staircase. This final indignity so infuriated him that he decided on one last attempt to uphold his dignity and social rank. The next night he would confront the insolent young Etonians in his celebrated role of 'Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl.'

He had not worn this disguise for over seventy years, not since using it to terrify pretty Lady Barbara Modish. So frightened had she been that she abruptly ended her engagement to the current Lord Canterville's grandfather and eloped to Gretna Green with handsome Jack Castleton. Nothing on earth, she declared, would persuade her to marry into a family that permitted such a dreadful apparition to pace the terrace at twilight.

"Jupiter," he said upon our reaching the tree's foot, "come here. Was the skull fastened to the bough with its face turned outward, or turned against the wood?"

"Face out, massa, so the crows could reach the eyes easy, without no trouble."

"Then was it through this eye or that one that you let the beetle fall?" Legrand here touched Jupiter's eyes in succession.

"This one, massa—the left one—just like you said." The eye Jupiter pointed to, however, was his right.

"Enough; we shall have to try once more."

My friend, in whose apparent madness I now discerned, or imagined I discerned, some definite method, shifted the peg marking the beetle's landing place some three inches westward. He again stretched the measuring tape from the nearest part of the trunk to the peg and extended it directly onward for fifty feet. This marked a position several yards from our earlier excavation.

A circle slightly wider than the first was drawn about the new spot, and we resumed our work with the spades. Though terribly fatigued, I no longer felt much resentment of the labour, and could scarcely explain the alteration in my feelings. An unaccountable interest, indeed an excitement, had taken hold of me. Perhaps something beneath Legrand's extravagant behaviour, some suggestion of planning or considered purpose, had impressed me. I dug eagerly, sometimes surprising myself by watching with almost genuine expectation for the imagined treasure whose prospect had deranged my poor companion. When these wandering fancies were most strongly upon me, and we had worked perhaps an hour and a half, the dog's furious howls interrupted us again. His earlier agitation had evidently sprung from play or whim; now its note was harsh and earnest. When Jupiter once more attempted to muzzle him, he resisted fiercely, sprang into the excavation, and clawed madly at the soil. Within a few seconds he exposed a heap of human bones belonging to two entire skeletons, mixed with several metal buttons and what seemed the powder of rotted woollen fabric. A stroke or two of a spade brought up the blade of a large Spanish knife. Further digging revealed three or four scattered coins of gold and silver.
